title: First Missing Positive
corePattern: In-Place Hashing / Cyclic Sort (Index as Hash Key)
interviewTips: Ask if O(n) time and O(1) extra space is required - this rules out hash set and sorting and points to index-as-hash.
Trade-off: hash set is simplest O(n) time O(n) space, sorting is O(n log n) time O(1) space, cyclic placement is optimal O(n) time O(1) space but mutates input.
Edge cases to mention: all negatives and zeros, duplicates, out-of-range large values, [1] -> 2, and [1,2,...,n] -> n+1.

approaches.name: Approach 1: Brute Force Check 1..n+1
approaches.intuition: By pigeonhole principle the answer must be in range 1 to n+1. Try k=1,2,3... and linearly scan to see if k exists, return first missing.
approaches.theory: With n numbers, the set {1..n+1} has n+1 values so at least one is missing. Checking each candidate with a linear scan is correct but repeats work, leading to quadratic time.

timeComplexity.explanation: Up to n+1 candidates, each requires O(n) scan in worst case.

spaceComplexity.explanation: Only a few variables besides input.

edgeCases: TLE for n=1e5 due to quadratic time

approaches.name: Approach 2: Sorting + Single Scan
approaches.intuition: Sort the array so all positives appear in order, then sweep once tracking the smallest expected missing value.
approaches.theory: After sorting, duplicates and non-positives can be skipped. Maintain miss starting at 1: if x < miss skip, if x == miss increment miss, if x > miss we found gap and can stop.

timeComplexity.explanation: Dominated by sorting; single linear scan after.

spaceComplexity.explanation: In-place sort aside from stack; strictly O(log n) stack in C++/Java and O(n) in Python Timsort.

steps: miss=1 sees -1 skip, sees 1 -> miss=2, sees 3 > 2 -> break

approaches.name: Approach 3: Index as Hash (Cyclic Placement)
approaches.intuition: Use array index itself as hash: value v in [1,n] belongs at index v-1. Swap each such value to its home, then first index i where nums[i] != i+1 is answer.
approaches.theory: If nums[i] is in [1,n] and not already at correct place, swap it with nums[nums[i]-1]. Each swap places at least one element correctly, so total swaps O(n). After placement, presence of k is equivalent to nums[k-1]==k. Values <=0 or >n are ignored as they can never be answer except via gap.

timeComplexity.explanation: Each index visited once and each swap fixes at least one position, so total swaps and checks are linear.

spaceComplexity.explanation: In-place rearrangement using only constant extra variables.

steps: i=0 val 3 swap to index2 -> [ -1,4,3,1 ] then -1 out of range stop
i=1 val 4 swap to index3 -> [-1,1,3,4] then swap index1 with index0 -> [1,-1,3,4]
scan: index0 ok, index1 has -1 !=2 -> return 2

edgeCases: Duplicates [1,1] must check nums[target]!=nums[i] to avoid infinite loop
